task_description: A math word problem. Assume every research article Nature published in 2020 used statistical significance to justify its findings, and that on average those tests came to a p-value of 0.04. The p-value IS the probability that a 'significant' finding is a false positive, so 0.04 (4%) of the articles would be wrong in their significance claim. The task wants: 4% of the 2020 Nature article count, rounded up to the next integer. The gold answer 41 corresponds to 0.04 * ~1001 articles = 40.04 -> ceil = 41.
final_vs_expected: produced None (FINAL ANSWER never emitted; run hit message cap) vs gold 41 — team never performed the 0.04 * 1001 = ceil(40.04) computation and never finalized.
primary_cause: The team collectively misread the problem as 'is 0.04 below the 0.05 cutoff?' and declared the count 'not determinable from the average alone,' then looped that non-answer until the message cap without ever multiplying 0.04 by the article count or emitting a FINAL ANSWER.
mast_rationale: 1.5 (Unaware of termination conditions): the Finalizer NEVER emits 'FINAL ANSWER'; from turn 7 onward it repeats 'What still needs to be done: the question setter must clarify...' and the run dies at the ~30-message cap with no answer. 3.1 (Premature termination / non-termination): no resolution path — the team locked into 'underdetermined' and stopped making progress while still consuming turns. 1.3 (Step repetition): turns 5,10,13,19,20,23,25,28 (Analyst) and 7–27 (Finalizer) republish near-identical 'not determinable' / 'needs clarification' text verbatim, dozens of times. 2.2 (Fail to ask for clarification, mis-applied): every agent KEEPS saying the question setter must clarify an interpretation, but in a closed group chat there is no human to ask — they treat a solvable problem as blocked on absent input instead of just solving it. Note: the named 'Final answer:' selector concern in the prompt did not occur in this transcript; the selector always routed to a member, so no selector-emitted final answer to scrutinize.
trace_narrative: Turn 1: Selector picks WebResearcher. It searches and fetches the Nature 2020 research-articles page, correctly extracting 'Article (1001)' for 2020 — a usable article count. But in its round-3 reasoning it talks itself out of the real math ('If p-values are uniformly distributed... 4% could be significant, but I'm confused... maybe none are actually incorrect?') and PUBLISHES 'Answer: 0 papers' on the grounds that 0.04 < 0.05. Turn 2: Critic correctly rejects '0' as unjustified — but for the wrong reason: it frames the issue as 'an average doesn't tell you the distribution,' demanding the question setter clarify whether 0.04 is per-paper or an average. Neither agent recognizes that p=0.04 directly gives a 4% false-positive rate. Turns 3–5: Analyst (3 turns) parrots 'not determinable from the average alone; if every paper had p=0.04 then 0.' Turn 6: Critic re-reviews, repeats the same 'underdetermined' verdict. Turn 7–18: Selector ping-pongs between Finalizer and Analyst; Finalizer repeatedly publishes the identical 'question setter must clarify...' stub and NEVER emits FINAL ANSWER, because its rule is 'only finalize after critic concerns are resolved' and the (unresolvable, self-imposed) concern is never cleared. Turns 19–28: the loop continues — Analyst and Finalizer republish verbatim non-answers; several rounds emit no reasoning at all. Turn 29: Critic gives one last 'cautious and consistent, but underdetermined' review. The run exhausts its message budget with no FINAL ANSWER.
open_ended_diagnosis: This is fundamentally a shared single-agent capability/conceptual error, amplified into a non-terminating loop by a brittle Finalizer gate. The conceptual error: the entire team misframes the question. The intended (and standard) reading is that a p-value is the false-positive probability, so an average p of 0.04 means ~4% of the significance claims are false positives; 4% of 1001 articles = 40.04 -> ceil = 41. EVERY agent instead anchors on the irrelevant comparison '0.04 < 0.05, so the paper is significant,' which answers a different question. The WebResearcher even had the correct ingredient (1001 articles) in hand and still could not assemble the multiplication. Once the team mislabeled the problem 'underdetermined / needs the question setter to clarify,' it created a permanent blocker: in a closed MAS there is no question setter to respond, so the Critic's demand can never be satisfied and the Finalizer's 'only finalize when concerns are resolved' rule guarantees it never finalizes. The result is structural non-termination layered on top of the capability error. Crucially, the inter-agent channel did NOT distort information — the 1001 count and the 0.04/0.05 facts propagate faithfully through every published message. The agents agree with each other perfectly; they are collectively, correctly transmitting a wrong frame. So the dominant cause is capability (everyone solves the wrong problem), with a secondary harness/role-design failure (Finalizer never recognizes it must emit an answer, treating 'ask the absent human' as a valid action).
reasoning_vs_published: The private-vs-published gap is small here — reasoning and published text are tightly aligned (low distortion), which is itself the diagnostic: the failure is not lossy communication but shared wrong understanding. WebResearcher's round-3 reasoning explicitly wavers — 'If p-values are uniformly distributed, with an average of 0.04, it seems that out of 1001 articles, 4% could be significant, but I'm confused' — it brushes against the correct 4% framing, then abandons it and publishes the categorical 'Answer: 0 papers'. That is the one near-miss where the right idea existed privately and did not survive to the published message, but it is reasoning-internal abandonment, not deliberate withholding. The Finalizer's reasoning repeatedly states 'we should only finalize after addressing any critiques... there are unresolved issues... pause for now' (turns 15, 35-style stubs) and its action matches — so no 2.6 reasoning-action mismatch; the action faithfully executes a flawed rule. The Critic's reasoning ('the average alone doesn't determine how many individual papers were above 0.05') is published almost verbatim — again no distortion, just a wrong premise faithfully relayed. The selector reasoning reveals the trap at turn 26: 'my routing rule states that after a proposed answer, I should route to Critic... it seems the next step should indeed be Critic, even though it's a bit circular' — the selector itself recognizes the loop and routes into it anyway. Verification theater (false-trust) appears in the Critic repeatedly stamping the non-answer as 'cautious and consistent' (turns 6, 26, 29) — it validates the FORM of careful hedging while the SUBSTANCE (an actual count) is never produced, and never challenges the team's core misreading of what a p-value means.
